title: Where Human Sleep Went Wrong
gist: Interview with evolutionary anthropologist David Samson, author of The Sleepless Ape, on how Hadza hunter-gatherers report high sleep satisfaction despite short, fragmented sleep, challenging both the Paleo sleep hypothesis and Western medical orthodoxy about unbroken sleep.

insights.claim: Among the Hadza tribe of northern Tanzania, evolutionary anthropologist David Samson observed that sleep was highly fragmented, short in duration, and low in efficiency (actual sleep time versus time in bed), largely because camp activity, storytelling, food-sharing, and dancing continued late into the night.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Real-world hunter-gatherer sleep patterns look nothing like the idealized long, deep, uninterrupted sleep often prescribed by modern sleep medicine.
insights.quote: Their sleep was highly fragmented, short in duration, and low in “efficiency,” or actual time spent sleeping versus time in bed.
insights.locator: When evolutionary anthropologist David Samson was living

insights.claim: Despite fragmented, short, low-efficiency sleep, the Hadza uniformly reported high satisfaction with their sleep quality.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the assumption that sleep quality can be measured by duration and continuity alone, challenging metrics used in consumer sleep-tracking and clinical sleep medicine.
insights.quote: Yet, the Hadza uniformly reported high satisfaction with their sleep.
insights.locator: This broken sleep was partly the consequence

insights.claim: The Hadza's satisfaction with fragmented sleep challenges the “Paleo sleep hypothesis,” the notion that hunter-gatherer sleep must be optimally long and deep, while also running counter to Western medical orthodoxy that unbroken sleep is essential for a good night's rest.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Suggests two competing sleep narratives — the romanticized Paleo ideal and modern medical dogma — are both contradicted by direct fieldwork among a living hunter-gatherer population.
insights.quote: It challenged the so-called Paleo sleep hypothesis, the notion that hunter-gatherer sleep must be optimally long and deep, but also ran counter to the medical orthodoxy that unbroken sleep is essential to a good night’s rest.
insights.locator: When evolutionary anthropologist David Samson was living

insights.claim: David Samson set out to resolve the “sleep paradox”: sleep is critical to human functioning, yet humans sleep fewer total hours than any other ape while still being arguably the most evolutionarily successful primate.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Reframes human sleep evolution as an efficiency story rather than a duration story — humans may have evolved to sleep less but better, with implications for how sleep health should be judged.
insights.quote: we sleep fewer total hours than any other ape, and are still arguably the most evolutionarily successful of the primates

insights.claim: Samson's research, drawn from fieldwork including studying chimpanzee tree nests and sleeping huts and practices across communities in Africa and Madagascar, is compiled in his new book The Sleepless Ape: The Story of Sleep in Human Evolution.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Signals a forthcoming popular-science book synthesizing comparative primate and cross-cultural human sleep research, relevant to anyone tracking sleep-science and evolutionary anthropology literature.
insights.quote: The stories he collected, people he met, and research findings he uncovered are vividly described in his new book The Sleepless Ape: The Story of Sleep in Human Evolution.
